diag:data.summary:
I worked read-only in /Users/Krishna/.cache/vector-token-efficiency. Fetch plus fast-forward took the worktree to 9d899636f. origin/main then moved to dd8a87049, which changes only web and Codium-page files, so I fast-forwarded to it as well. The benchmark data is unchanged. I made no code changes, ran no tests, made no model calls and did not touch Codex's data.

The scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-Krishna-Vectordev-ai/82c740c0-7c7a-4353-9c97-5f74368e9da6/scratchpad/tokan/: lib.py, perreq.py (per-request tokens), timing.py, cf.py (counterfactuals), disc.py (round4 discovery) and paths.py. Prices are the archive's gpt-6.1-sol rates per million tokens: $2 uncached input, $0.10 cached input, $10 output.

Per-request data exists only in two files: patched-vs-codex/latency-analysis.json (9 vs 9 runs, 44 vs 38 requests) and next-efficiency/runtime-bench/latency-analysis.json (18 vs 18 runs, 87 vs 75 requests). The other rounds only have per-run totals.

HEADLINE: Vector's gap to Codex is almost entirely its first request. Within a session Vector caches as well as Codex. Leaving out the first request and full cache misses, Vector's cached share is 0.895 (patched) and 0.929 (next-efficiency); Codex's is 0.906 and 0.924. Vector also sends about half the tokens per request: first request about 8.4–8.6K tokens against Codex's 16.2K, later requests about 10.2–10.5K against 17.5–18.0K.

The difference is in the first request:
- **Vector:** zero cached tokens on 20 of 27 measured first requests, and on 25 of 27 in the round4 discovery-v3 review. When something was cached it was always exactly 4,864 tokens.
- **Codex:** 12,288 cached tokens on 27 of 27 first requests.
- **How much it costs:** Vector's first request is 41.5% of a run's cost (median, round4 review). Uncached tokens on the first request explain 77% of Vector's uncached-input gap in the patched comparison and more than 100% of it in next-efficiency.
- **Cached share by turn, patched:** Vector 0.19 / 0.87 / 0.89 / 0.83 / 0.79 for turns 0–4; Codex 0.76 / 0.96 / 0.88 / 0.91 / 0.78.
- **Cached share by turn, next-efficiency:** Vector 0.15 / 0.91 / 0.83 / 0.87 / 0.96; Codex 0.76 / 0.95 / 0.89 / 0.92 / 0.96.

Counterfactual: if Vector reused just the 4,864-token prefix on every first request, the patched gap would shrink from +25.6% to +5.7%. Next-efficiency would go from +16.4% to Vector 8% cheaper ($0.483 vs $0.526). If the whole fixed prefix were reused, Vector would be 14–29% cheaper than Codex.

RANKED BY $ (per run, sol medium):
1. **First-request prefix not reused across sessions:** +$0.0057–0.0067 per run of uncached input.
2. **Extra output tokens:** +$0.0033 per run in the patched comparison, mostly literal 12-file patches. This fell to +$0.0006 after round 2.
3. **One extra request per task**, a separate check turn after each edit: +0.67 requests per run, about $0.0036–0.0041.
4. **Title side request:** Codex has none. In round4 it was 1.8–4.8% of a Vector run's cost, about $0.0014 per run on sol.
5. **Mid-session full cache misses:** same token cost as Codex in this data. But a Vector miss falls to 0 cached, while a Codex miss still gets the 12,288-token prefix.

Vector's smaller prompts save it $0.0028 per run in cached reads. Do not give that up.

RANKED BY SECONDS (median wall: patched 24.0 s vs 16.6 s; next-efficiency 25.7 s vs 20.1 s):
1. **Writing long multi-file edits as literal patches:** the refactor edit turn took 14–16 s against Codex's 3.6–5.3 s, about 10 s on that task. Round 2 cut the refactor run from 37.8 s to 28.6 s.
2. **Extra request:** about 2.8–3.2 s per run.
3. **Final answer:** span is 1.0–1.4 s longer (3.56 vs 2.22 s and 3.69 vs 2.67 s). The final message is 86–89 tokens against Codex's 61–62.
4. **Slow first request:** 1.27–1.37 s from request start to the first stream event, against 0.60–0.67 s on later requests. That is a fresh TLS connection plus 8.4K uncached prompt tokens.
5. **Time before the first model request:** 2.17–2.31 s against Codex's 1.53–1.66 s (median). Vector took 5–13 s in 5 of 27 runs; Codex's worst was 2.8 s. The merged lazy-catalog change (54e64107f) made the first provider request 1.21x slower.
6. **Client time after each response:** about 0.13–0.2 s per request between the provider's last event and Vector closing the step, so 0.7–1.0 s per task.
7. **One 174-second stalled first request** (test-writing, attempt 2).

Not bottlenecks: gaps between a tool result and the next request are 6–13 ms in total per run. Tool time is 0.3 s per run faster than Codex, and exit is 0.6–0.7 s faster.

Memory is 3–4x Codex's: 912–964 MiB against 244–310. Nearly all of it is Vector's own process: about 0.5 GB for an empty session, and the full provider catalog adds 367 MiB.

WHAT EACH CODEX ROUND MOVED:

**Round 1, prompt efficiency** (Vector-only A/B on 10-07):
- Requests 64 → 44 (7.1 → 4.9 per run), todo-only calls 20 → 0, output 10,882 → 8,121 tokens.
- Total tokens −31%, median time 38.5 → 23.9 s, cost −8.2% ($0.4195 → $0.3850).
- Uncached input rose 129,399 → 136,512 and cached share fell 80.0% → 69.3%. It removed cheap cached tokens and left the expensive first request alone.

**Round 2, next-efficiency patch:**
- The refactor task now uses script edits: output 1,589 → 813 tokens, time 37.8 → 28.6 s.
- Cost ratio against Codex on the original 3 tasks went from 1.26 to 1.15; cached share 73.4% → 77.4%.
- First requests were still uncached in 14 of 18 runs.

**Round 3:**
- Vector's cost on the original tasks rose 29% ($0.2808 → $0.3634) while Codex stayed flat; cost ratio 1.52 on those tasks, 0.97 on the held-out ones.
- Cached share fell to 67.8%. All 18 title requests failed.
- The data has no per-request detail, so I cannot say why.

**Round 4:**
- **Discovery runs:** across 9 model/effort combinations, Vector's cost relative to Codex ranged 0.80–1.43 and was higher in 5 of them; it was close to or below Codex only at max effort. First request still uncached; titles now have a known cost.
- **Lazy catalog:** memory 0.75x but first provider request 1.21x slower (2.56 → 3.10 s).
- **Unmeasured:** a separately measured provider-fastpath variant (−16% first request, −22% memory) is not the one cited for 54e64107f. The prompt trim (−6,006 bytes, mostly cached tokens) is not measured on its own. Removing prompt_cache_key and lower text verbosity (both in 6e2a7b4f1) were merged without a matched measurement.

None of the rounds fixed the first-request cache, which is the largest cost.

Caveats:
- n=3 per task. Codex's own cost on the same 3 tasks moved 12–14% between back-to-back sessions ($0.2788, $0.2447, $0.2387).
- I cannot tell from these files whether the reused 4,864 tokens are the tool definitions or the instructions before the environment block, so the exact cutoff is unverified.

causes.cause: Vector's fixed prompt prefix is not reused across sessions on the first request. The env block (working directory, date, references and user system text) sits inside `instructions` for ChatGPT sign-in (llm/request.ts: options.instructions = system.join), or in the leading system messages on the API path. Through d3ae064a2, prompt_cache_key was also the session ID (transform.ts), so each session got its own cache routing key. Codex keeps its instructions and tools byte-stable and puts its environment in the input.
causes.impact:
Largest by $.

**Gap it explains:**
- Patched: Vector's first requests left 61,263 tokens uncached against Codex's 35,448, which is +2,868 tokens per run, +$0.0057 per run, and 72% of the total $0.0714 gap.
- Next-efficiency: 131,665 against 71,016, which is +3,369 tokens per run and +$0.0067 per run. That is 140% of the total gap: without it Vector would be cheaper.

**Counterfactuals:**
- A, always reusing the 4,864-token shared prefix: saves $0.0062 per run (patched) and $0.0072 per run (next-efficiency). Vector would cost $0.295 against Codex's $0.279, and $0.483 against $0.526.
- B, reusing the whole fixed prefix with about 400 first-request tokens left uncached: saves $0.0122–0.0132 per run. Vector would cost $0.241 against $0.279, and $0.376 against $0.526.

**Time:** about +0.7 s on the first request (first-event lag 1.27–1.37 s against 0.60–0.67 s on later requests; this also includes TLS setup).

**Subagents:** every subagent starts its own session cold, so this cost repeats for each one.
causes.evidence:
**First-request caching:**
- Patched: Vector cached 0 on 6 of 9 first requests and exactly 4,864 on 3 (first request about 8,428 tokens). Codex cached 12,288 on 9 of 9 (first request about 16,227).
- Next-efficiency: Vector cached 0 on 14 of 18, 4,864 on 3, and 8,576 on 1. That last one is the run whose first step took 174 s, probably a retry inside the same session. Codex cached 12,288 on 18 of 18.
- round4 v4-next-performance-review: zeroCacheReads 25 of 27 trials. The first main request is 41.5% of a trial's cost (median); its input median is 8,462 tokens.

**Within-session caching is fine:** leaving out the first request and full misses, Vector's cached share is 0.895 and 0.929 against Codex's 0.906 and 0.924. The pure append delta per later request is the same for both, about 890 tokens (patched).

**Request shape** (round4 request-shape-diagnostic-v3):
- Two sessions in the same directory differ only in a 30-byte body key plus 3 session headers.
- A different directory also changes `instructions` from byte 15,402 of 16,343.
- Tools (24,773 bytes, 59% of the 41,706-byte body; task 9,375, bash 5,020, todowrite 3,064) are identical.

**Harness:** the fixture directory is unique per run (harness/runner.ts: runs/<id>/<task>/<attempt>/<runtime>/fixture).
causes.fix:
1. **Measure the prompt_cache_key removal in 6e2a7b4f1 now.** Use a local two-session probe against the documented Responses shape, then one matched live pair. Read cached_tokens on the first request of session B, in the same directory and in a different one, on both the ChatGPT sign-in and API-key paths.
2. **Move everything per-session out of `instructions` and the leading system messages.** That means env (cwd and date), references, AGENTS.md and the user system text. Send it as a developer input item after the stable instructions and tools. Then the cross-session prefix is provider prompt + stable system + tools, the way Codex does it.
3. **Keep the tool schemas byte-stable and in a fixed order.** They already are; add a test.
4. **Verify on the real wire:** session 2's first request should show cached ≥ 8K tokens when the prefix is warm.
causes.risk_to_quality:
Low. Nothing is dropped; the same text moves later in the prompt.

The model may weight environment facts and AGENTS.md rules slightly differently as a developer message than as instructions. Keep them in the developer role and re-run the prompt-seam and behaviour suites. Codex uses this layout. Cache retention depends on the provider, so savings will be smaller after long idle gaps.

causes.cause: More output tokens per task. Vector writes mechanical multi-file changes as literal patches; Codex uses a short script edit. Vector's final message and its text before tool calls are also wordier.
causes.impact:
**Cost:**
- Patched: +3,004 output tokens over 9 runs (902 against 568 per run), +$0.0033 per run, 42% of the gap. Almost all of it is refactor-structured-logging (1,589 against 491 tokens median).
- After round 2: +1,027 over 18 runs (714 against 657 per run), +$0.0006 per run, 12% of the gap.

**Time:**
- The refactor edit turn takes 14.0–16.4 s against Codex's edit-and-check of 3.6–5.3 s, about 10 s per refactor run (about 3.5 s per run averaged over the patched set).
- The final message is 86–89 against 61–62 tokens.
- Text Vector streams before tool calls takes 0.9–1.4 s per run.

Reasoning tokens are negligible on both sides at medium effort: Vector 10–20 per run, Codex 0–36.
causes.evidence:
- **Patched latency analysis, refactor:** Vector's edit message has 925–930 output tokens and 3,221 characters of tool input. Codex's edit-and-check input is 562–761 characters.
- **next-efficiency originalLoggingRefactor:** the script-pattern edit is detected; refactor output median 813 and wall median 28.6 s, against 37.8 s in the patched run.
- **Discovery at max effort:** Codex produces more output (1,775–2,293 against 1,227–1,584 tokens per run), and that is where the cost ratio reaches 0.75–1.00.
causes.fix:
- Keep the round-2 guidance: use a scripted transform plus a diff check for repetitive multi-file edits. Confirm it survived into 6e2a7b4f1.
- Measure textVerbosity=low (merged, but not matched against Codex) on final summaries.
- Do not cut the information content of the final report.
causes.risk_to_quality:
Medium. A sed- or perl-style script can match too much. Mitigate with the scoped diff review that already runs and the test pass.

Terser final answers can drop details users rely on; check them against the behaviour suite (which was at 15 of 18 at the E12 check).

causes.cause: One extra provider request per task. Vector runs the edit and the verification in separate turns (edit, result, new request to run tests). Codex does edit-and-check in one turn.
causes.impact:
**Requests per run:** +0.67 in both datasets (4.89 against 4.22 patched; 4.83 against 4.17 next-efficiency). Round3: 5.5 against 4.6. The original comparison was 6.44 against 4.00, before round 1 removed the todo-only turns.

**Cost:** a typical mid-session Vector request costs $0.0053–0.0062, so this is $0.0036–0.0041 per run.

**Time:** median mid-session span is 4.2–4.8 s, so about 2.8–3.2 s per run.
causes.evidence:
**Patched:** Codex combined edit and check in 9 of 9 runs, for example check → inspect → edit-and-check → final. Vector did edit then a separate check in 9 of 9, for example check → inspect → edit → check → final-text.

**Next-efficiency:** Codex combined them in 18 of 18. Vector kept them separate in 15 of 18; the other 3 still had a turn after the edit.

**Round 1:** dropping the TodoWrite-every-turn rule took requests from 64 to 44 and todo calls from 20 to 0.
causes.fix:
- Let the model emit the edit and its targeted check in one response.
- Guarantee that a bash call in the same step runs only after any mutating call (apply_patch, edit, write) has finished.
- Add one prompt line allowing "apply the edit and run the targeted check in the same response".
causes.risk_to_quality:
Medium. If the calls are not strictly ordered, the test can run against the code before the edit and give a false pass or fail. Ordering has to be enforced in code, not just in the prompt.

Verification must never be skipped. Behaviour tests should assert that a check still runs after every edit.

causes.cause: The title side request (Codex sends none). Since 6e2a7b4f1, ChatGPT sign-in also runs titles on the primary model.
causes.impact:
About $0.0014 per run on gpt-6.1-sol, 1.8–4.8% of a Vector run's cost (round4 discovery, all 9 model/effort combinations). On gpt-6-astra it is about $0.0068 per run.

It starts about 0.2 s before the main request (round4 layer timing: first LLM call median 1,752 ms, main median 1,959 ms). The data does not show whether it delays the main request. The title call itself takes a median of 3.0 s and runs concurrently with the main request.
causes.evidence:
- round3 latency analysis: 18 title requests, all 18 failed, median 522 ms, usage unknown. In the Oct 7–8 matched runs titles failed, so their cost was not counted.
- round4 discovery v1/v3/v4: 1 extra request per Vector run with known cost, which disc.py splits out using rates fitted from Codex runs.
- Local fixture (lazy-provider-ab): 2 requests per task, a 2,492-byte title request and a 41.9 KB main request.
causes.fix:
- Build the title locally from the prompt, or send the title request only after the first main request is on the wire.
- Use the cheapest allowed model and a stable cached prefix for titles.
- Skip titles for headless and CLI runs.
causes.risk_to_quality: None for coding quality. Titles get somewhat worse until the model-generated title arrives.

causes.cause: Time before the first model request and other client-side latency. This covers startup (imports, catalog, tools, services), cold TLS on the first request, startup outliers, and about 130–200 ms of Vector-side time after each response's last event (post-transport tail).
causes.impact:
**Startup:** +0.5–0.8 s per run at the median (Vector 2.17–2.31 s against Codex's turn context at 1.53–1.66 s). Vector took 5–13 s in 5 of 27 runs (11.2 s in patched; 5.3, 5.9, 8.9 and 13.5 s in next-efficiency); Codex's worst was 2.8 s.

**After each response:** 0.13–0.2 s per request, or 0.7–1.0 s per task.

**Lazy-catalog change (54e64107f):** made the first provider request slower, from 2,560 to 3,104 ms (1.21x median, 1.37x paired geometric mean).

**One long-tail stall:** a first request took 174 s.
causes.evidence:
- **Patched and next-efficiency:** processToFirstAssistantMs against processToTurnContextMs.
- **round3:** preFirstLLMScopeMs 2.1–2.9 s. A new socket on 18 of 99 requests (one per trial), connect median 394 ms.
- **round4 layer timing:** stepFinishToScopeCloseMs median 126 ms, postTransportTail median 140 ms per request.
- **round4 v4 review:** postTransportTail median 204 ms per request; startupBeforeMain median 2,274 ms.
- **provider-startup-benchmark-v1:** the lazy-catalog numbers above.
- **provider-fastpath-ab:** first request 1,880 → 1,573 ms (−16%), wall −11%.
- **snapshot-deferral-v6:** first request −6%.
- **startup-comparison** (a light command, not a session): vector-native 283 ms and vector-source 518 ms against codex-native 13 ms.
causes.fix:
- Open the TLS connection to the provider at startup, in parallel with session setup.
- Move to the next step as soon as the provider's terminal event arrives (usage comes with it) instead of waiting for the stream to close.
- Combine the lazy catalog with the fastpath variant, so memory goes down without slowing the first request.
- Find the cause of the 5–13 s startup outliers.
causes.risk_to_quality: Low. Make sure usage and cost are still recorded from the terminal event, so spend is not under-counted.

causes.cause: Process memory: Vector's own process (Bun runtime, imports, provider catalog, services).
causes.impact: Median peak 912–964 MiB, against Codex's 244–310 MiB (3–4x). There is no direct $ cost; it matters for footprint on users' machines and for parallel agents.
causes.evidence:
**Matched runs:** original 964 vs 244, patched 935 vs 310, next-efficiency 912 vs 277, round3 865–889 vs 240–287, discovery 651–953 vs 210–317 MiB.

**Where it goes:**
- Child processes add only 5–12 MiB in the local fixture.
- An empty-control session uses 476–544 MiB; the full catalog adds +367 MiB and +628 ms (catalog-attribution).
- RSS by phase: 147 MiB after imports, 348 MiB when services are ready.

**Fixes already measured:** lazy catalog 0.75x, fastpath 0.78x, snapshot deferral 0.93x.
causes.fix: Keep the lazy catalog, but use the fastpath variant so the first request does not slow down. Add the snapshot deferral. Then profile the remaining 0.5 GB at the cli.imports and services.ready phases.
causes.risk_to_quality: None for coding quality. Lazy loading can surface missing-model errors later in a session, so keep the catalog tests.

causes.cause: Mid-session full cache misses (provider-side eviction or routing).
causes.impact:
Net about $0 against Codex in this data. Vector's extra uncached tokens from misses were 25,600 against Codex's 23,424 (patched) and 32,640 against 32,384 (next-efficiency).

But a Vector miss resends the whole prompt at once: 9.6–10.9K uncached tokens, about $0.02 each. Codex misses fall back to its globally cached 12,288-token prefix.
causes.evidence: Patched: Vector had 2 full misses (cached 0 after a cached turn) and 1 partial; Codex had 0 full and 4 partial. Next-efficiency: Vector 3 full; Codex 0 full and 6 partial.
causes.fix: The first-request prefix fix covers this too: a miss would then fall back to the shared stable prefix instead of zero.

diag:requests.summary:
Short answer: when I compare the requests byte for byte, Vector and Codex build OpenAI Responses requests that cache equally well within a session. Nothing before the newest turn changes between requests in Vector: no timestamps, no re-sent environment block, no todo or state injection and no reordering. The extra uncached input in the live benchmark comes from three things: how the request is sent, whether the cache is warm when a session starts, and how requests are routed. Codex has all three covered and Vector does not.

WHAT I RAN (all offline, fake model server, isolated HOME, no network, no paid calls, nothing committed; worktree /Users/Krishna/.cache/vector-token-efficiency is unchanged at 7148a7a0e)
- The requested command, run under `env -i PATH HOME=<scratch>`, so Codex's `--version` check never saw the real HOME and Vector did not inherit PWD: `bun script/agent-eval/footprint.ts --runtime vector,codex --codex …/codex --out …/scratchpad/footprint-openai.json`. Exit 0. Log: …/scratchpad/fp/base-openai.log.
- A scratch copy of the harness, …/scratchpad/fp/footprint-ext.ts, built on the earlier agent's extension. It adds:
  - a `vector-openai` runtime, so Vector is measured on the OpenAI Responses API rather than Anthropic;
  - request and header dumps;
  - reasoning items with encrypted_content;
  - `--pwdfix`;
  - a sandboxed `--version` check;
  - `--cmodel`;
  - `--ws`, a WebSocket Responses endpoint.
- Runs:
  - vector-openai vs codex, all 4 scenarios, with reasoning (fp/ext-openai-reasoning.json);
  - a second solo-fix of each, for cross-session diffs (fp/ext-openai-r2.json);
  - both runtimes on model gpt-6.1-sol (fp/ext-g6.json);
  - Codex over WebSocket (fp/ext-ws.json);
  - vector vs claude-code, all scenarios plus a second solo-fix (fp/ext-anthropic.json, fp/ext-an2.json).
- Analysis scripts: fp/analyze.py (anatomy of each request and how far its prefix matches the previous one), fp/crossdiff.py (cross-session diff), fp/anth.py (Anthropic cache breakpoints).
- Disclosure: before setting up the sandbox, I ran `codex --version` once directly in my own shell. That only prints the version and does not read config, and it was the only time Codex ran outside the sandbox.

REQUEST ANATOMY: OPENAI (gpt-5.5 fake model, one session; "tok" is the harness estimate of characters/4)
- **Vector, API-key path**
  - No `instructions` field. input[0] is one developer message of 12,134–12,265 characters:
    - gpt.txt plus the stable policies take up characters 0–11,062.
    - Then the per-session `<env>` block: Working directory at about character 11,144, date at about 11,412.
    - Then the skills list.
  - 9 tools, 23,344 characters (5,836 tok). The task tool alone is 1,987 tok, bash 1,266, todowrite 605. Tools are sorted alphabetically and are byte-identical across sessions.
  - Body fields: store:false; include:[reasoning.encrypted_content]; reasoning {effort: medium, summary: auto}; text.verbosity: low; tool_choice: auto. prompt_cache_key is the session ID on gpt-5.5, but absent on gpt-6.1-sol since 6e2a7b4f1.
  - Not sent: parallel_tool_calls (server default), truncation, previous_response_id.
  - Headers: session-id, x-session-affinity, x-session-id.
  - Every earlier reasoning item is handed back with encrypted_content and its summary. Vector strips item IDs; Codex keeps them, but IDs are not prompt text.
- **Vector, ChatGPT sign-in path** (taken from the code; the plugin's endpoint is fixed, so it cannot be captured offline)
  - packages/engine/src/session/llm/request.ts:102, `if (isOpenaiOauth) options.instructions = system.join("\n")`, puts the whole system prompt into `instructions`. That includes the per-session cwd, date, AGENTS.md, MCP and skills.
  - Release builds use HTTP. Local/dev/beta builds use WebSockets (plugin/index.ts:62), but ws.ts:331 still sends the full payload each time and never uses previous_response_id.
- **Codex 0.162.0-alpha.2** (the version in the live benchmark; captured in the earlier 09:25 dump)
  - `instructions` is a static 21,299-character base prompt.
  - 10 tools, 9,510 characters (2,378 tok).
  - input: a developer message with skills and permissions (5,162 characters; only HOME-dependent paths vary), then a user message with `<environment_context>` holding cwd and date, then the task.
  - Body fields: parallel_tool_calls:true, store:false, the same include, prompt_cache_key equal to the thread ID, text.verbosity: low, client_metadata. Headers: session-id and thread-id.
- **Codex 0.162.0-alpha.17.2** (the binary installed now)
  - Same content, with the base prompt moved into input[0] as a developer message.
  - On gpt-6.1-sol it sends tools as an `additional_tools` input item (25,347 characters, a "code mode" exec tool plus namespaces), `reasoning: {effort: low, context: "all_turns"}`, `parallel_tool_calls: false`, and still sends prompt_cache_key equal to the thread ID.

PREFIX STABILITY
- Within a session, every main-agent and subagent request in every scenario fully extends the previous request (checked with analyze.py over the whole serialized prefix). That holds for vector-openai, codex, vector on Anthropic and claude-code. No bytes before the newest turn ever change.
- Across sessions, Vector's first request differs only at the cwd inside `<env>`: all 23,344 characters of tools plus 11,352 characters of the developer message are identical. Codex differs only in the skills path, which is a harness artifact because HOME is a temp folder, and in the environment_context cwd.
- With an idealised implicit cache and HTTP on both sides, offline cost is level: solo-fix $0.0489 vs $0.0480, long-loop $0.0862 vs $0.0852. With delegation Vector costs more because each subagent's first request starts cold: delegate-explore $0.0642 vs $0.0527, delegate-general $0.0575 vs $0.0529.
- Conclusion: the bytes in Vector's requests do not cause the live gap.

WHAT CODEX DOES THAT VECTOR DOES NOT (captured with the `--ws` fake, handshake header `OpenAI-Beta: responses_websockets=2026-02-06`)
- Request 1 is a warmup: `generate:false` with only the tools and the static base prompt.
- Request 2 is the full input.
- Requests 3–6 each send only the single new function_call_output, with `previous_response_id: resp_N`.

ANTHROPIC, FOR REFERENCE (vector vs claude-code)
- Both extend the prefix fully on every turn.
- **Vector:** system is two blocks, 12,096 stable characters then 1,072 per-session characters. Tools are 25,477 characters, 10 definitions. Four cache breakpoints: both system blocks, the last tool_use and the last tool_result.
- **Claude Code:** system blocks of 74, 62 and 28,011 characters. Tools are 84,831 characters, 24 definitions. Three breakpoints, thinking enabled, plus context_management. Its per-project memory path and git status sit in the middle of its large system block.
- **Cost:** Vector is about 2.9 times lighter. Solo-fix: 51,521 vs 151,464 tokens, $0.0557 vs $0.1533. Long-loop: $0.0837 vs $0.2231. Fixed tokens per request: 9,623 vs 27,917.

HARNESS PROBLEMS FOUND
- footprint.ts passes `{...process.env}` to Vector, so `vector run` takes the root from the inherited `process.env.PWD` (cli/cmd/run.ts:337). Vector then runs in the Vector worktree instead of the test fixture, and the 09:24 run in the scratchpad was affected. Fix: add `PWD: dir` to vectorEnv.
- `--runtime vector,codex` puts Vector on Anthropic Messages and prices it at Sonnet rates, while Codex is on OpenAI. Those numbers do not compare like with like.
- The `--version` check runs Codex with the inherited environment.
- The harness's pricing does not model WebSocket requests or previous_response_id.
- The fake server cannot drive Codex's GPT-6 `additional_tools` mode.

SIDE NOTE
- `vector run` wraps any argument containing a space in literal quotes and escapes the quotes inside it (run.ts:291-293), so the model receives the prompt text in quotation marks.

causes.cause: The first request of every Vector session is cold: nothing is cached for it, while Codex's static prefix is already warm.
causes.impact: 61,263 of Vector's 118,182 uncached input tokens across the 9 live patched runs (52%), about $0.117 at $2/M. In 6 of 9 runs the first request had 8,406–8,466 uncached and 0 cached tokens. In the other 3 it had 3,542–3,602 uncached and 4,864 cached. Codex's whole-run uncached input is only 5,658–8,589 tokens in 7 of 9 runs, so its first request must be mostly cached.
causes.evidence: Live: docs/benchmarks/vector-codex-2026-10/data/patched-vs-codex.metrics.json, per-message uncachedInputTokens and cacheReadTokens. Offline: crossdiff.py shows Vector's tools plus the first 11,352 characters of its system text are identical across sessions (about 8K tokens), so Vector is not missing a stable prefix. Codex's prefix is the same for every Codex user on that version (21,299-character instructions plus 9,510-character tools). Codex also warms it at session start: the captured request 1 of fp/dump-ws/codex-solo-fix.json has `generate:false` with only tools and the base prompt. Vector sends no warmup. On the ChatGPT sign-in path, request.ts:102 puts the whole system prompt, including per-session cwd, date, AGENTS.md and skills, into `instructions`. If the server renders instructions before tools, as OpenAI's published harmony format does, then the roughly 5.4K tokens of tools come after per-session bytes and can never be shared across sessions; on the API-key path tools come first. The observed 4,864-token cross-session hit is smaller than Vector's byte-stable prefix, and the archive has no request bodies, so the hosted rendering order cannot be confirmed offline.
causes.fix: (a) On the ChatGPT sign-in path, put only the provider prompt plus env.stable into `instructions`, and send the per-session block (env, AGENTS.md, MCP, skills) as a developer input item, the same split Codex uses. (b) Over the per-session WebSocket, send a `generate:false` warmup at session start with tools plus the stable instructions, and count its usage in tokenomics. (c) Live-test `prompt_cache_retention: "24h"` on GPT-5.1+. Upper-bound savings: 29K–54K uncached tokens per 9 runs, $0.055–$0.103, which is 16–29% of Vector's $0.350.
causes.risk_to_quality: (a) Low to none: the model sees the same text, only moved from instructions to a developer message, as Codex already does. Run the prompt-seam and behaviour tests. (b) No quality effect, but each session gets one extra prefill that must be counted, never hidden. (c) None.

causes.cause: Mid-session cache resets on a request whose prefix is byte-identical to the one before it. Vector re-sends the full conversation over stateless HTTP, while Codex continues on the same WebSocket connection with previous_response_id.
causes.impact: About 24.5K uncached tokens (21%), about $0.047. Two requests got 0 cached tokens: 10,863 (bugfix attempt 1, request 5) and 9,638 (feature attempt 2, request 4). One fell back to 4,864 cached (refactor attempt 1, request 2: 4,393 uncached). Those are the two runs where Vector reached 2–3 times Codex's uncached input: 21,673 vs 5,658 and 19,756 vs 5,981.
causes.evidence: Offline, every Vector request fully extends the previous one in all scenarios (fp/analyze.py on fp/dump-oa-r, fp/dump-an), so these misses come from server-side routing or eviction, not from bytes. Codex 0.162 over WebSocket (fp/dump-ws): handshake `OpenAI-Beta: responses_websockets=2026-02-06`, and requests 3–6 carry `previous_response_id: resp_N` with only the single new function_call_output item. The Codex binary contains the strings responses_websockets_v2, previous_response_id, prewarm and warmup. Vector release builds use HTTP (plugin/index.ts:62-64, WebSockets only on local/dev/beta), and plugin/openai/ws.ts:331 sends `{type:'response.create', ...fullPayload}` with no previous_response_id. Each Vector request also uploads 36–44KB, where Codex sends about 1KB.
causes.fix: Add incremental continuation to plugin/openai/ws.ts and ws-pool.ts. When the new input equals the previous input plus the previous output items plus new items, send `previous_response_id` and only the new items. Fall back to a full resend on any mismatch, a dropped socket or previous_response_not_found. Then enable WebSockets by default for ChatGPT sign-in. Add a fake-server test using the `--ws` shape from fp/footprint-ext.ts.
causes.risk_to_quality: None if the fallback is exact, because the model sees the same conversation. The risk is correctness, such as a wrong response ID or lost state, which the full-resend fallback covers. Keep the engine suite and the WebSocket transport tests green.

causes.cause: 6e2a7b4f1 stopped sending prompt_cache_key for OpenAI GPT-5.6+ and GPT-6 (transform.ts:1166-1177), while Codex still sends it.
causes.impact: Not measured: the live benchmark used d3ae064a2, which still sent the key. Could increase resets once usage is concurrent.
causes.evidence: Captured on gpt-6.1-sol (fp/dump-g6): Vector's body has no prompt_cache_key. Codex 0.162.0-alpha.17.2 sends prompt_cache_key equal to the thread ID on gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-5.5, plus session-id and thread-id headers. OpenAI's prompt-caching guide says routing hashes the first ~256 tokens of the prefix together with the key. Without a key, all Vector sessions share one routing group, because their first 256 tokens are identical. Above roughly 15 requests per minute for one prefix and key, requests spill over to other machines. A single live Vector session already ran about 13–14 requests per minute (5 requests in about 22 seconds). The review records that Codex's own probe saw 0 cached tokens in both conditions.
causes.fix: Send prompt_cache_key equal to the session ID for every OpenAI model, as Codex does, and keep the `setCacheKey:false` opt-out. If the cross-session argument in the code comment is to be tested, run a live A/B comparing cached_tokens on request 1 and request N.
causes.risk_to_quality: None, it is routing metadata only.

causes.cause: Vector does not send `reasoning.context: "all_turns"` for GPT-6; Codex does.
causes.impact: No effect on the single-prompt benchmark, where everything is one user turn. In conversations with follow-up prompts, it could cost a near-full re-read of history on every new prompt, if the server's default (current_turn) drops earlier reasoning items from what it renders. That is a hypothesis.
causes.evidence: Captured Codex gpt-6.1-sol body: `reasoning: {effort: low, context: "all_turns"}`. The binary contains the enum strings current_turn and all_turns. Vector's gpt-6.1-sol body has `reasoning: {effort: medium, summary: auto}` only.
causes.fix: For GPT-6, send reasoning.context:'all_turns' where the endpoint accepts it. First run a two-turn live check comparing cached_tokens on the second user turn with and without it.
causes.risk_to_quality: Probably positive, because the model keeps its earlier reasoning, at the cost of more context tokens, mostly read from cache. Needs measurement.

causes.cause: Vector's fixed tool definitions are 2.5 times the size of Codex's: 23,344 characters vs 9,510.
causes.impact: Every request reads them from cache. They are paid at full price on each cold first request and on each subagent's first request. Offline, delegation costs Vector 9–22% more than Codex, while single-agent loops are level.
causes.evidence: fp/ext-openai-reasoning.log, tool definitions in estimated tokens: task 1,987, bash 1,266, todowrite 605, read 434, apply_patch 385, grep 355, webfetch 305, glob 265, skill 156. Codex's whole tool set is 2,297.
causes.fix: Shorten task.txt first (34% of tool bytes), then bash. Do this only behind the agent behaviour tests.
causes.risk_to_quality: Real: delegation and tool-use guidance could get worse. Do not cut anything the model needs. Prove it with the behaviour and agent-eval suites.

causes.cause: Not caching: Vector writes more output tokens than Codex.
causes.impact: +$0.030 of the $0.071 cost gap (8,120 vs 5,116 output tokens). The refactor task shows it most: 1,589 vs 491 output tokens.
causes.evidence: patched-vs-codex summary: Vector input $0.236, cache reads $0.033, output $0.081. Codex input $0.169, cache reads $0.058, output $0.051.
causes.fix: Separate investigation into what the extra output is (patch text, todo calls, final report).
causes.risk_to_quality: Depends on what is cut. Do not shorten required deliverables.

causes.cause: Minor: the date is recomputed on every step, a title request is sent per session, and the prompt is wrapped in quotes.
causes.impact: Small. Each title request is about 680 estimated tokens and below the 1,024-token cache minimum, so it is never cached. When a session crosses midnight, the whole prefix is invalidated once.
causes.evidence: system.ts:254 rebuilds `new Date().toDateString()` on every step inside the system text, while Codex keeps the date in its environment_context user message. The side request appears in every vector-openai dump. run.ts:291-293 wraps the prompt in literal quotes.
causes.fix: Fix the date when the session starts, and add a new context note when it changes. Leave the title request as is: it is counted honestly now.
causes.risk_to_quality: None for a date fixed per session, as long as date changes are announced to the model.
